claim: The DISFA dataset contains facial videos recorded at 20 frames per second from 27 participants who viewed a 4 min video consisting of short emotive clips from YouTube.
source: The DISFA dataset contains facial videos recorded at 20 frames per second from 27 participants who viewed a 4 min video consisting of short emotive clips from YouTube (Mavadati et al., 2019; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section describing the DISFA dataset, with citation to the original source.

claim: Time-frequency representations of individual participants capture high-frequency dynamics that are obscured by characterising group-averaged time courses.
source: This demonstrates that the time-frequency representations of individual participants capture high-frequency dynamics that are obscured by characterising group-averaged time courses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 1, where individual time-frequency representations showed significantly greater amplitude at higher frequencies compared to the group mean time series.

claim: Compared to the group mean time series, the time series of individuals had significantly greater amplitude, particularly at higher frequencies.
source: Compared to the group mean time series, the time series of individuals had significantly greater amplitude (Figure 1b), particularly at higher frequencies (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical comparison and visualized in Figure 1b and 1f.

claim: Stimulus-evoked facial action unit responses have asynchronous alignment across participants, hence cancelling when superimposed.
source: This is because stimulus-evoked facial action unit responses have asynchronous alignment across participants, hence cancelling when superimposed.
evidence: This is provided as an explanation for why individual time-frequency representations preserve high-frequency content that is lost in group averaging.

claim: An HMM infers a set of distinct states from noisy observations, with each state expressed sequentially in time according to state-to-state transition probabilities.
source: An HMM infers a set of distinct states from noisy observations, with each state expressed sequentially in time according to state-to-state transition probabilities.
evidence: This is a description of the HMM methodology used in the study.

claim: Inferred state sequences had high between-subject consistency, exceeding chance level across the vast majority of time points and reaching 93% during specific movie events.
source: We found that inferred state sequences had high between-subject consistency, exceeding chance level across the vast majority of time points and reaching 93% during specific movie events (Figure 3d).
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3d comparing observed consistency to null distribution.

claim: State transition probabilities appeared clustered by valence rather than frequency.
source: State transition probabilities appeared clustered by valence rather than frequency, such that frequent transitions between low- and high-frequency oscillations of the same facial action units were more likely than transitions between different emotions (Figure 3e).
evidence: This pattern is observed in the transition probability graph shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The melancholia dataset comprises 30 participants with major depressive disorder who were recruited from the specialist depression clinic at the Black Dog Institute in Sydney, Australia.
source: The melancholia dataset comprises 30 participants with major depressive disorder who were recruited from the specialist depression clinic at the Black Dog Institute in Sydney, Australia.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the melancholia cohort.

claim: Participants with melancholia met criteria for a current major depressive episode and were diagnosed as having the melancholic subtype.
source: These participants met criteria for a current major depressive episode, were diagnosed as having the melancholic subtype by previously detailed criteria (Taylor and Fink, 2006), and did not have lifetime (hypo)mania or psychosis (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the diagnostic criteria for the melancholia cohort, with citation to the diagnostic criteria used.

claim: A significant three-way interaction was found between clinical group, stimulus, and facial valence (p=0.003).
source: A significant three-way interaction was found between clinical group, stimulus, and facial valence (p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the three-way ANOVA analysis.

claim: During stand-up comedy, participants with melancholia had reduced activation of action unit 12 'Lip Corner Puller' (p<0.0001).
source: Post hoc comparisons with Tukey's honestly significant difference criterion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) quantified that during stand-up comedy, participants with melancholia had reduced activation of action unit 12 'Lip Corner Puller' (p<0.0001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post hoc comparisons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: During stand-up comedy, participants with melancholia had increased activation of action unit 4 'Brow Lowerer' (p<0.0001).
source: during stand-up comedy, participants with melancholia had reduced activation of action unit 12 'Lip Corner Puller' (p<0.0001) and increased activation of action unit 4 'Brow Lowerer' (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post hoc comparisons.

claim: Facial responses of participants with melancholia during stand-up comedy were similar to those of controls during the sad movie.
source: Interestingly, facial responses of participants with melancholia during stand-up comedy were similar to those of controls during the sad movie (p>0.05 for both action units).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing no significant difference between these two conditions.

claim: Participants with melancholia had a complex pattern of reduced activity encompassing a broad range of frequencies.
source: Participants with melancholia had a complex pattern of reduced activity encompassing a broad range of frequencies (Figure 5a).
evidence: This pattern is shown in the time-frequency difference maps in Figure 5a.

claim: The most prominent differences were in positive valence action units during positive valence stimuli.
source: The most prominent differences were in positive valence action units during positive valence stimuli, but significant reductions were seen in most action units.
evidence: This describes the pattern of group differences observed in the time-frequency analysis.

claim: There were sporadic instances of increased activity in melancholia participants during the sad movie involving mainly action units 15 'Lip Corner Depressor' and 20 'Lip Stretcher'.
source: There were sporadic instances of increased activity in melancholia participants during the sad movie involving mainly action units 15 'Lip Corner Depressor' and 20 'Lip Stretcher'.
evidence: This describes specific findings from the time-frequency analysis during the sad movie stimulus.

claim: A support vector machine using mean action unit activation for each stimulus video as inputs achieved 63% accuracy with five-fold cross-validation.
source: A support vector machine, using as inputs the mean action unit activation for each stimulus video, achieved 63% accuracy with five-fold cross-validation.
evidence: This is a reported classification accuracy from machine learning analysis.

claim: Using mean time-frequency amplitude in discrete frequency bands within 0–5 Hz as inputs improved average cross-validation accuracy to 71% (p<0.001 for difference between models).
source: In contrast, using as inputs the mean time-frequency amplitude in discrete frequency bands within 0–5 Hz improved average cross-validation accuracy to 71% (p<0.001 for difference between models).
evidence: This is a reported classification accuracy showing significant improvement over the baseline model.

claim: Models using mean action unit activations within shorter time blocks had 63–64% accuracy despite having a greater number of input features than the time-frequency representation.
source: These models had 63–64% accuracy despite having a greater number of input features than the time-frequency representation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that the improved accuracy of time-frequency models is not simply due to having more features.

claim: Between-subjects consistency was markedly reduced in the melancholic participants during both funny videos.
source: The temporal sequence of the most common state was similar across groups (Figure 6c), but the between-subjects consistency was markedly reduced in the melancholic participants during both funny videos (Figure 6d).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 6d comparing consistency between control and melancholia groups.

claim: Fractional occupancy was significantly different between groups for positive valence state 1 (Melancholia < Controls, pFDR = 0.03).
source: Fractional occupancy – the proportion of time spent by participants in each state – was significantly different between groups for the positive valence states – state 1 (Melancholia < Controls, pFDR = 0.03)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the HMM state occupancy analysis.

claim: Fractional occupancy was significantly different between groups for positive valence state 2 (Melancholia < Controls, pFDR = 0.004).
source: state 2 (Melancholia < Controls, pFDR = 0.004)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the HMM state occupancy analysis.

claim: Fractional occupancy was significantly different between groups for negatively valenced state 8 (Melancholia > Controls pFDR = 0.03).
source: as well as for negatively valenced state 8 (Melancholia > Controls pFDR = 0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the HMM state occupancy analysis.

claim: Participants with melancholia were significantly less likely to switch from a low-frequency positive valence state (1, smiling) to high-frequency positive valence oscillations (state 2, giggling).
source: Participants with melancholia were significantly less likely to switch from a low-frequency positive valence state (1, smiling) to high-frequency positive valence oscillations (state 2, giggling), but were more likely to switch to states associated with any other emotion (states 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8).
evidence: This describes differences in state transition probabilities between groups.

claim: From the high-frequency positive valence state, participants with melancholia were more likely to switch to the deactivating 'ennui' state 4.
source: From the high-frequency positive valence state, they were more likely to switch to the deactivating 'ennui' state 4 (all pFDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about state transition probabilities in the melancholia group.

claim: Facial expressions are critical to interpersonal communication and offer a nuanced, dynamic, and context-dependent insight into internal mental states.
source: Facial expressions are critical to interpersonal communication and offer a nuanced, dynamic, and context-dependent insight into internal mental states.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of facial expressions, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Humans use facial affect to infer personality, intentions, and emotions.
source: Humans use facial affect to infer personality, intentions, and emotions, and it is an important component of the clinical assessment of psychiatric illness.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of facial affect in human social cognition and clinical practice.

claim: Facial affect is an important component of the clinical assessment of psychiatric illness.
source: Humans use facial affect to infer personality, intentions, and emotions, and it is an important component of the clinical assessment of psychiatric illness.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical practice in psychiatry.

claim: A traditional approach is to count the occurrences of a discrete list of 'universal basic emotions'.
source: A traditional approach is to count the occurrences of a discrete list of 'universal basic emotions' (Ekman, 1992).
evidence: This describes a traditional approach in the field, with citation to Ekman's work.

claim: The most commonly used system designates six basic emotions.
source: While the most commonly used system designates six basic emotions, there is disagreement about the number and nature of such affective 'natural forms' (Ortony, 2022; Keltner et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the traditional basic emotions approach, with citations noting ongoing debate.

claim: There is disagreement about the number and nature of affective 'natural forms'.
source: While the most commonly used system designates six basic emotions, there is disagreement about the number and nature of such affective 'natural forms' (Ortony, 2022; Keltner et al., 2019).
evidence: This acknowledges ongoing debate in the field, with citations to recent discussions.

claim: Quantifying facial affect using the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) has become the dominant technique to operationalise facial expressions.
source: Quantifying facial affect using the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) has become the dominant technique to operationalise facial expressions (Ekman et al., 1978).
evidence: This describes the dominance of FACS in the field, with citation to the original work.

claim: In FACS, action units each correspond to an anatomical facial muscle group and are rated on a quantitative scale.
source: Action units, each corresponding to an anatomical facial muscle group, are rated on a quantitative scale.
evidence: This describes the structure of the FACS system.

claim: Traditional emotion labels are associated with the co-occurrence of a specific set of action units.
source: Traditional emotion labels are associated with the co-occurrence of a specific set of action units – for example, a 'happy' facial expression corresponds to action units 'Cheek Raiser' and 'Lip Corner Puller' (Friesen and Ekman, 1983).
evidence: This describes how FACS relates to emotion categories, with citation to the EMFACS system.

claim: Due to the time-intensive nature of manually coding every frame in a video, FACS has traditionally been applied to the analysis of static pictures rather than videos of human faces.
source: However, due to the time-intensive nature of manually coding every frame in a video, FACS has traditionally been applied to the analysis of static pictures rather than videos of human faces.
evidence: This explains a practical limitation of traditional FACS application.

claim: Recent developments in machine learning can assist the identification of basic emotions and facial action units from images and videos of human faces.
source: Recent developments in machine learning can assist the identification of basic emotions and facial action units from images and videos of human faces.
evidence: This describes recent technological advances in the field.

claim: Feature extraction for images include local textures and 3D geometry.
source: Feature extraction for images include local textures (Feng, 2004; Kumar et al., 2016) and 3D geometry (Tian et al., 2001; Ghimire and Lee, 2013)
evidence: This describes feature extraction methods with citations to relevant work.

claim: Video analysis benefits from temporal features such as optical flow.
source: while video analysis benefits from temporal features such as optical flow (Yeasin et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes methods for video analysis with citation.

claim: Supervised learning algorithms classifying basic facial expressions based on feature values have achieved accuracies of 75–98% when benchmarked against manually coded datasets of both posed and spontaneous expressions.
source: Supervised learning algorithms classifying basic facial expressions based on feature values have achieved accuracies of 75–98% when benchmarked against manually coded datasets of both posed and spontaneous expressions (Ekundayo and Viriri, 2019).
evidence: This reports performance metrics from the literature with citation.

claim: Videos of faces can now be transformed into action unit time series which capture the rich temporal dynamics of facial expressions.
source: Videos of faces can now be transformed into action unit time series which capture the rich temporal dynamics of facial expressions (Tian et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes current capabilities in facial analysis with citation.

claim: Human faces express emotional states dynamically – such as in a giggle or a sob.
source: This is important because human faces express emotional states dynamically – such as in a giggle or a sob.
evidence: This is a statement about the dynamic nature of facial expressions.

claim: Some psychological studies and databases have asked responders to pose discrete emotions such as happiness or sadness.
source: For example, some psychological studies and databases have asked responders to pose discrete emotions such as happiness or sadness (Lucey et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a common approach in the field with citation.

claim: Posed discrete emotions suit the needs of a classic factorial experimental design but fail to produce the natural dynamics of real-world facial expressions.
source: This strategy suits the needs of a classic factorial experimental design but fails to produce the natural dynamics of real-world facial expressions.
evidence: This is a critique of posed emotion approaches based on their ecological validity.

claim: To evoke dynamic emotion, clinical interviews have been used.
source: To evoke dynamic emotion, clinical interviews have been used (Darzi et al., 2019), or participants have been asked to narrate an emotive story or been shown emotive pictures rather than videos (Lang et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes alternative approaches to evoking emotion with citations.

claim: There is an expanding interest in using participants' facial responses to naturalistic video stimuli.
source: Consequently, there is an expanding interest in using participants' facial responses to naturalistic video stimuli (Kollias et al., 2019; Mavadati et al., 2019; Soleymani et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a trend in the field with citations to recent work.

claim: Naturalistic video stimuli are more ecologically valid than posed emotions.
source: These are more ecologically valid, have greater test-retest reliability than interviews, evoke stronger facial expressions than static pictures, and produce stronger cortical responses during functional neuroimaging (Ambadar et al., 2005; Sonkusare et al., 2019; Schultz and Pilz, 2009).
evidence: This lists advantages of naturalistic stimuli with citations to supporting research.

claim: Naturalistic video stimuli have greater test-retest reliability than interviews.
source: These are more ecologically valid, have greater test-retest reliability than interviews, evoke stronger facial expressions than static pictures, and produce stronger cortical responses during functional neuroimaging (Ambadar et al., 2005; Sonkusare et al., 2019; Schultz and Pilz, 2009).
evidence: This lists advantages of naturalistic stimuli with citations to supporting research.

claim: Naturalistic video stimuli evoke stronger facial expressions than static pictures.
source: These are more ecologically valid, have greater test-retest reliability than interviews, evoke stronger facial expressions than static pictures, and produce stronger cortical responses during functional neuroimaging (Ambadar et al., 2005; Sonkusare et al., 2019; Schultz and Pilz, 2009).
evidence: This lists advantages of naturalistic stimuli with citations to supporting research.

claim: Naturalistic video stimuli produce stronger cortical responses during functional neuroimaging.
source: These are more ecologically valid, have greater test-retest reliability than interviews, evoke stronger facial expressions than static pictures, and produce stronger cortical responses during functional neuroimaging (Ambadar et al., 2005; Sonkusare et al., 2019; Schultz and Pilz, 2009).
evidence: This lists advantages of naturalistic stimuli with citations to supporting research.

claim: Interpreting participants' facial expressions resulting from naturalistic stimulus viewing poses challenges, because each time point is unique.
source: However, interpreting participants' facial expressions resulting from naturalistic stimulus viewing poses challenges, because each time point is unique.
evidence: This identifies a methodological challenge with naturalistic stimuli.

claim: There is currently no obvious way to parse the stimulus video into discrete temporal segments.
source: There is currently no obvious way to parse the stimulus video into discrete temporal segments.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current methodology.

claim: Averaging action unit activations across time omits temporal dynamics and fails to capture the complexity of natural responses.
source: Naïve attempts at dimensionality reduction – for example, averaging action unit activations across time – omit temporal dynamics and so fail to capture the complexity of natural responses.
evidence: This is a critique of simple averaging approaches based on what information they lose.

claim: Disturbances in facial affect occur across a range of mental health disorders, including major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, and dementia.
source: Disturbances in facial affect occur across a range of mental health disorders, including major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, and dementia.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical manifestations of mental health disorders.

claim: Capturing the nuances of facial affect is a crucial skill in clinical psychiatry but in the absence of quantitative tests this remains dependent on clinical opinion.
source: Capturing the nuances of facial affect is a crucial skill in clinical psychiatry but in the absence of quantitative tests this remains dependent on clinical opinion.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in current clinical practice.

claim: Supervised learning has shown promise in distinguishing people with major depression from controls.
source: Supervised learning has shown promise in distinguishing people with major depression from controls, using input features such as facial action units coded manually (Cohn et al., 2009) or automatically (Gavrilescu and Vizireanu, 2019), or model-agnostic representations of facial movements such as the 'Bag of Words' approach (Dibeklioğlu et al., 2015; Bhatia et al., 2017a).
evidence: This describes previous work in automated depression detection with citations.

claim: Depression is associated with reduced frequency of emotional expressions, particularly expressions with positive valence.
source: Studies documenting action unit occurrence during the course of a naturalistic stimulus (Renneberg et al., 2005), a short speech (Trémeau et al., 2005), or a clinical interview Girard et al., 2014 have demonstrated that depression is associated with reduced frequency of emotional expressions, particularly expressions with positive valence.
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous studies with citations.

claim: By averaging action unit occurrence over time, previous methods poorly operationalise the clinician's gestalt sense of affective reactivity.
source: Unfortunately, by averaging action unit occurrence over time, these methods poorly operationalise the clinician's gestalt sense of affective reactivity, which derive from a patient's facial responses across a range of contexts.
evidence: This is a critique of previous methods based on what clinical information they fail to capture.

claim: The approach presented is data-driven, eschewing the need to preselect emotion categories or segments of the stimulus video.
source: The approach is data-driven, eschewing the need to preselect emotion categories or segments of the stimulus video.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the proposed methodology.

claim: The time-frequency representation improves accuracy in classifying patients from healthy controls.
source: The time-frequency representation improves accuracy in classifying patients from healthy controls.
evidence: This is a summary of the classification results comparing time-frequency to baseline approaches.

claim: The use of spectral features of facial action units facilitates easy interpretation while also exploiting prior knowledge to reduce the need for very large training datasets.
source: However, unlike end-to-end deep learning approaches, our use of spectral features of facial action units facilitates easy interpretation while also exploiting prior knowledge to reduce the need for very large training datasets.
evidence: This describes advantages of the proposed approach compared to deep learning.

claim: Dynamic facial patterns reveal specific changes in melancholia, including reduced facial activity in response to emotional stimuli.
source: Dynamic facial patterns reveal specific changes in melancholia, including reduced facial activity in response to emotional stimuli, anomalous facial responses inconsistent with the affective context, and a tendency to get 'stuck' in negatively valenced states.
evidence: This summarizes key findings about melancholia from the study.

claim: Dynamic facial patterns reveal anomalous facial responses inconsistent with the affective context in melancholia.
source: Dynamic facial patterns reveal specific changes in melancholia, including reduced facial activity in response to emotional stimuli, anomalous facial responses inconsistent with the affective context, and a tendency to get 'stuck' in negatively valenced states.
evidence: This summarizes key findings about melancholia from the study.

claim: Dynamic facial patterns reveal a tendency to get 'stuck' in negatively valenced states in melancholia.
source: Dynamic facial patterns reveal specific changes in melancholia, including reduced facial activity in response to emotional stimuli, anomalous facial responses inconsistent with the affective context, and a tendency to get 'stuck' in negatively valenced states.
evidence: This summarizes key findings about melancholia from the study.

claim: Frame-by-frame action unit activations were extracted with OpenFace software.
source: Frame-by-frame action unit activations were extracted with OpenFace software (Baltrusaitis et al., 2018) (see Supplementary file 1 for action unit descriptions, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for group mean time series).
evidence: This describes the software used for action unit extraction with citation.

claim: The continuous wavelet transform was used to extract a time-frequency representation of individual action unit time series in each participant.
source: From these data, we used the continuous wavelet transform to extract a time-frequency representation of individual action unit time series in each participant.
evidence: This describes the method used for time-frequency analysis.

claim: Action unit 12 'Lip Corner Puller' is conventionally associated with happy affect.
source: We selected the activity of action unit 12 'Lip Corner Puller' during a positive valence video clip (a 'talking dog'), as this action unit is conventionally associated with happy affect
evidence: This is a statement about conventional associations in FACS.

claim: High-frequency activity of action unit 12 denotes smiling or laughing.
source: as this action unit is conventionally associated with happy affect, and its high-frequency activity denotes smiling or laughing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what high-frequency activity in this action unit represents.

claim: The group-level time-frequency representation avoids the problem of asynchronous alignment by extracting amplitude at the individual level prior to group averaging.
source: This problem is avoided in the group-level time-frequency representation, whereby the amplitude is first extracted at the individual level, prior to group averaging.
evidence: This explains how the time-frequency approach solves the alignment problem.

claim: Comparable results to those shown for action unit 12 occurred in all action units.
source: Comparable results occurred in all action units (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This indicates that the findings generalize across action units, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: An HMM was inferred from the time course of all facial action units' time-frequency representations.
source: Having shown how the time-frequency representation captures dynamic content, we next sought to quantify the joint dynamics of facial action units. To this end, an HMM was inferred from the time course of all facial action units' time-frequency representations.
evidence: This describes the next step in the analysis pipeline.

claim: Each HMM state has a distinct mapping onto the input space of frequency bands and action units.
source: Each state has a distinct mapping onto the input space, here the space of frequency bands and action units
evidence: This describes a property of the HMM states.

claim: State occurrence corresponded strongly with annotated video clip valence.
source: Their occurrence corresponded strongly with annotated video clip valence (Figure 3b).
evidence: This describes the relationship between inferred states and stimulus properties, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: States were frequency-localised and comprised intuitive combinations of action units.
source: States were frequency-localised and comprised intuitive combinations of action units which reflected not only distinct emotion categories as defined in previous literature (Friesen and Ekman, 1983), but also stimulus properties such as mixed emotions.
evidence: This describes properties of the inferred HMM states with citation to EMFACS.

claim: HMM states reflected not only distinct emotion categories as defined in previous literature, but also stimulus properties such as mixed emotions.
source: States were frequency-localised and comprised intuitive combinations of action units which reflected not only distinct emotion categories as defined in previous literature (Friesen and Ekman, 1983), but also stimulus properties such as mixed emotions.
evidence: This describes how the inferred states relate to both traditional emotion categories and more complex affective states.

claim: Frequent transitions between low- and high-frequency oscillations of the same facial action units were more likely than transitions between different emotions.
source: State transition probabilities appeared clustered by valence rather than frequency, such that frequent transitions between low- and high-frequency oscillations of the same facial action units were more likely than transitions between different emotions (Figure 3e).
evidence: This describes the pattern of state transitions observed in the data.

claim: The melancholia cohort watched three video clips consecutively – a stand-up comedy, a sad movie clip, and a non-English language video which is initially puzzling but also amusing.
source: We next analysed facial video recordings from a cohort of participants with melancholic depression and healthy controls who watched three video clips consecutively – a stand-up comedy, a sad movie clip, and a non-English language video which is initially puzzling but also amusing.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the melancholia study.

claim: The three stimuli were chosen from a database of independently rated videos of high salience.
source: These three stimuli were chosen from a database of independently rated videos of high salience (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the source and properties of the stimuli with citation.

claim: Clinical participants with melancholia were recruited from a tertiary mood disorders clinic and met melancholia criteria including psychomotor changes, anhedonia, and diurnal mood variation.
source: Clinical participants with melancholia were recruited from a tertiary mood disorders clinic and met melancholia criteria including psychomotor changes, anhedonia, and diurnal mood variation (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the clinical characteristics of the melancholia cohort.

claim: Facial action unit time courses showed clear group differences.
source: Facial action unit time courses showed clear group differences (see Figure 4 for action units typically implicated in expressing happiness and sadness, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 for all action units).
evidence: This summarizes the finding of group differences in action unit time courses.

claim: For each action unit in each participant, the median action unit activation was calculated across each stimulus video.
source: For each action unit in each participant, we calculated the median action unit activation across each stimulus video.
evidence: This describes the method for summarizing action unit activity.

claim: Happiness was defined as the sum of action units 6 'Cheek Raiser' and 12 'Lip Corner Puller'.
source: In keeping with previous work (Friesen and Ekman, 1983), we defined happiness as the sum of action units 6 'Cheek Raiser' and 12 'Lip Corner Puller'
evidence: This describes how happiness was operationalized, with citation to EMFACS.

claim: Sadness was defined as the sum of action units 1 'Inner Brow Raiser', 4 'Brow Lowerer', and 15 'Lip Corner Depressor'.
source: and sadness as the sum of action units 1 'Inner Brow Raiser', 4 'Brow Lowerer', and 15 'Lip Corner Depressor'.
evidence: This describes how sadness was operationalized, following EMFACS conventions.

claim: The time course of the first principal component across all action units closely followed joke punch lines during stand-up comedy.
source: The time course of this composite component closely followed joke punch lines during stand-up comedy (Figure 4b).
evidence: This describes the temporal relationship between the principal component and stimulus events.

claim: The responsivity of the first principal component to movie events was substantially diminished in the melancholia cohort.
source: This responsivity of this component to movie events was substantially diminished in the melancholia cohort.
evidence: This describes a group difference in the principal component analysis.

claim: For each action unit, the mean time-frequency representation for the control group was subtracted from the participants with melancholia.
source: For each action unit, the mean time-frequency representation for the control group was subtracted from the participants with melancholia
evidence: This describes the method for comparing time-frequency representations between groups.

claim: Significant group differences (p<0.05) were found by comparison to a null distribution composed of 1000 resampled surrogate datasets.
source: Significant group differences (p<0.05) were found by comparison to a null distribution composed of 1000 resampled surrogate datasets (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the statistical method for testing group differences.

claim: Significant reductions in facial activity in melancholia were seen in most action units.
source: The most prominent differences were in positive valence action units during positive valence stimuli, but significant reductions were seen in most action units.
evidence: This describes the breadth of group differences across action units.

claim: Differences in high-frequency bands occurred during specific movie events such as jokes.
source: Differences in high-frequency bands occurred during specific movie events such as jokes (Figure 5b).
evidence: This describes the temporal specificity of group differences in high-frequency activity.

claim: Inverting a HMM from the time-frequency representations of facial action units yielded the sequential expression of eight states across participants.
source: Inverting a HMM from the time-frequency representations of facial action units yielded the sequential expression of eight states across participants (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes the result of applying HMM to the melancholia dataset.

claim: The temporal sequence of the most common state was similar across groups.
source: The temporal sequence of the most common state was similar across groups (Figure 6c)
evidence: This describes a similarity between groups in state sequences.

claim: Some participants with melancholia had highly anomalous state sequences compared to other participants.
source: Some participants with melancholia – for example participants 2 and 3 (Figure 6b) – had highly anomalous state sequences compared to other participants.
evidence: This describes individual variability within the melancholia group.

claim: Participants with melancholia were more likely to switch from positive valence states to states associated with any other emotion.
source: Participants with melancholia were significantly less likely to switch from a low-frequency positive valence state (1, smiling) to high-frequency positive valence oscillations (state 2, giggling), but were more likely to switch to states associated with any other emotion (states 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8).
evidence: This describes differences in state transition patterns between groups.

claim: Facial expressions played a crucial role in the evolution of social intelligence in primates.
source: Facial expressions played a crucial role in the evolution of social intelligence in primates (Schmidt and Cohn, 2001) and continue to mediate human interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary importance of facial expressions with citation.

claim: Facial expressions continue to mediate human interactions.
source: Facial expressions played a crucial role in the evolution of social intelligence in primates (Schmidt and Cohn, 2001) and continue to mediate human interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about the current role of facial expressions in human social behavior.

claim: Observations of facial affect, its range, and reactivity play a central role in clinical settings.
source: Observations of facial affect, its range, and reactivity play a central role in clinical settings.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical practice.

claim: Quantitative analysis of facial expression has accelerated of late, driven by methods to automatically factorise expressions into action units and the availability of large datasets of posed emotions.
source: Quantitative analysis of facial expression has accelerated of late, driven by methods to automatically factorise expressions into action units (Ekman et al., 1978) and the availability of large datasets of posed emotions (Lucey et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes recent trends in the field with citations.

claim: The dynamics of facial expression mediate emotional reciprocity, but have received less attention.
source: The dynamics of facial expression mediate emotional reciprocity, but have received less attention (Ambadar et al., 2005).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature with citation.

claim: Naturalistic stimuli offer distinct advantages to affective research for their ability to evoke dynamic responses.
source: Naturalistic stimuli offer distinct advantages to affective research for their ability to evoke these dynamic responses (Dhall et al., 2012), but their incompressibility has made analysis problematic.
evidence: This describes an advantage of naturalistic stimuli with citation.

claim: The incompressibility of naturalistic stimuli has made analysis problematic.
source: Naturalistic stimuli offer distinct advantages to affective research for their ability to evoke these dynamic responses (Dhall et al., 2012), but their incompressibility has made analysis problematic.
evidence: This identifies a challenge with naturalistic stimuli.

claim: Analysis of healthy adults watching emotionally salient videos showed that facial expression dynamics can be captured by a small number of spatiotemporal states.
source: Analysis of healthy adults watching emotionally salient videos showed that facial expression dynamics can be captured by a small number of spatiotemporal states.
